mainTopic: Merit and sin, the greatness of Torah learning, and conduct that disqualifies a witness
overview: This amud opens with a teaching that a person should picture himself as exactly half guilty and half meritorious, so every single מצוה or עבירה tips his scale. רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון widens this to the whole world. רבי שמעון בן יוחי adds that a צדיק who rebels at the end loses his merits, and a רשע who does תשובה has his past erased. ריש לקיש explains that the צדיק loses his merits only if he regrets the good he did. A new משנה teaches that someone involved in מקרא, משנה and דרך ארץ will not quickly sin. The גמרא explains why צדיקים suffer and רשעים prosper in this world, using a tree parable. It then tells how the sages in לוד decided that learning is greater than doing, because learning leads to doing. It shows that learning comes first in time, in judgment and in reward. Finally it rules that a person lacking Torah and proper conduct, or one who eats in the marketplace, is unfit to be a witness. בר קפרא begins a teaching about an angry person that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Picture yourself as exactly half guilty and half meritorious
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא teaches that a person should see himself as perfectly balanced, so that one מצוה tips him to merit and one עבירה tips him to guilt, based on a פסוק in קהלת.
steps.simpleTranslation: A person should look at himself as if he were half guilty and half meritorious. If he does one מצוה, he is fortunate, because he tipped himself to the side of merit. If he does one עבירה, woe to him, because he tipped himself to the side of guilt. The פסוק says, 'One sinner destroys much good': because of one single sin, he loses a lot of good.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a way of looking at yourself: imagine your scale is exactly even, so your very next action decides which way it tips.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is not that every person really is exactly balanced. It is an attitude: if you picture yourself balanced, no single act is ever 'small,' because it alone can decide your judgment. The פסוק proves that one sin can cost a great deal of good.

keyTerms.meaning: Fortunate is he, happy is he
He tipped (the scale), he decided the balance
The side of the scale for merit / the side for guilt

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא is not saying every person really has an equal number of מצוות and עבירות. It says a person should view himself that way, so that he treats every action as decisive.

phrases.english: A person should view himself as though
he were half guilty and half meritorious.
If he did one מצוה, fortunate is he,
for he tipped himself to the side of merit.
If he committed one transgression, woe to him,
for he tipped himself to the side of guilt,
as it is said: "But one sinner destroys much good":
because of a single sin that he sinned,
much good is lost from him.

steps.triggerLanguage: יִרְאֶה אָדָם עַצְמוֹ כְּאִילּוּ חֶצְיוֹ חַיָּיב וְחֶצְיוֹ זַכַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opening statement of this section of the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person should treat himself as perfectly balanced, so that any single מצוה or עבירה decides his judgment.

steps.title: One person's deed can tip the whole world
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון adds that the world is also judged by its majority, so one person's single deed can tip both himself and the entire world.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון says: Because the world is judged by its majority, and each person is judged by his majority, if someone does one מצוה, he is fortunate, because he tipped himself and the whole world to merit. If he does one עבירה, woe to him, because he tipped himself and the whole world to guilt. The פסוק says, 'One sinner destroys...': because of the one sin this person did, much good was lost from him and from the whole world.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון takes the same 'balanced scale' idea and widens it from one person to the whole world.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new idea is that the world as a whole is also judged by whether most of its deeds are good or bad. So one person's single act can be the deciding weight for everyone, not just for himself. He reads the same פסוק as speaking about good lost from the whole world.
steps.whyThisMatters: This raises the stakes of every action: a person's single deed affects the judgment of the entire world, not only his own.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon says:
Since the world is judged according to its majority,
and the individual is judged according to his majority,
if he did one מצוה, fortunate is he,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהִכְרִיעַ אֶת עַצְמוֹ וְאֶת כָּל הָעוֹלָם לְכַף זְכוּת,
phrases.english: for he tipped himself and the entire world to the side of merit.
If he committed one transgression, woe to him,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהִכְרִיעַ אֶת עַצְמוֹ וְאֶת כָּל הָעוֹלָם לְכַף חוֹבָה,
phrases.english: for he tipped himself and the entire world to the side of guilt,
as it is said: "But one sinner, etc.":
phrases.notes: The כו׳ means 'and so on,' so finish the same פסוק from before: 'destroys much good.'

phrases.english: because of a single sin that this person did,

phrases.aramaic: אָבַד מִמֶּנּוּ וּמִכׇּל הָעוֹלָם טוֹבָה הַרְבֵּה.
phrases.english: much good was lost from him and from the entire world.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר: לְפִי שֶׁהָעוֹלָם נִידּוֹן אַחַר רוּבּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands the 'balanced scale' idea of step 1 from the individual to the whole world.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Because the world and the individual are both judged by majority, one deed can tip both oneself and the entire world.

steps.title: The end of a person's life decides: the rebelling צדיק and the returning רשע
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן יוחי teaches that a lifelong צדיק who rebels at the end loses his earlier merits, and a lifelong רשע who does תשובה at the end is no longer reminded of his wickedness, both from פסוקים in יחזקאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן יוחי says: Even someone who was a complete צדיק all his life but rebelled at the end loses his earlier good deeds, as the פסוק says, 'The righteousness of the righteous will not save him on the day of his sin.' And even someone who was a complete רשע all his life but did תשובה at the end is no longer reminded of his wickedness, as the פסוק says, 'And the wickedness of the wicked, he will not stumble over it on the day he turns from his wickedness.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון בן יוחי teaches that how a person ends up matters most, giving two opposite cases and a פסוק for each.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 1 and 2 were about counting and balancing deeds. Here a person's final direction can override his whole past: a צדיק who rebels loses his merits, and a רשע who does תשובה has his sins erased. This sets up the גמרא's question in the next step about why the past merits don't count.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says:
Even one who was completely righteous all his days
and rebelled at the end
has lost the earlier ones,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״צִדְקַת הַצַּדִּיק לֹא תַצִּילֶנּוּ בְּיוֹם פִּשְׁעוֹ״.
phrases.english: as it is said: "The righteousness of the righteous will not save him on the day of his transgression."
And even one who was completely wicked all his days
and repented at the end,
his wickedness is no longer mentioned to him,
as it is said: "And the wickedness of the wicked, he will not stumble over it
on the day he turns from his wickedness."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי אוֹמֵר: אֲפִילּוּ צַדִּיק גָּמוּר כׇּל יָמָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a different angle to the balance idea: one's final direction can override everything before it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A צדיק who rebels at the end loses his past merits; a רשע who does תשובה at the end is not reminded of his past sins.

steps.title: Shouldn't the rebelling צדיק at least be half and half?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי שמעון בן יוחי: a צדיק who sinned at the end should be judged as having half sins and half merits, not as having lost everything.
steps.simpleTranslation: But shouldn't he be like someone who has half sins and half merits?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבי שמעון בן יוחי's first case, the צדיק who rebelled at the end.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Based on the 'scale' idea from step 1, deeds get weighed. So a lifetime of מצוות should at least balance out the late sins. Why does רבי שמעון בן יוחי say he loses all his earlier merits?

keyTerms.meaning: Let him be, shouldn't he be

phrases.english: But let him be like one with half sins and half merits?
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the lifelong צדיק who rebelled at the end, from step 3.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְנִיהְוֵי כְּמֶחֱצָה עֲוֹנוֹת וּמֶחֱצָה זְכִיּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי שמעון בן יוחי's ruling about the צדיק who rebelled.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי שמעון בן יוחי's claim that a צדיק who rebels at the end loses all his earlier merits.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If deeds are weighed on a scale, past מצוות should still count and at least balance the late sins, not vanish completely.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: he regrets his earlier good deeds
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש answers that רבי שמעון בן יוחי is talking about someone who regrets the מצוות he did earlier, so they are no longer counted.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: It is talking about someone who regrets his earlier good deeds.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש answers the question by narrowing the case: this צדיק did not just sin, he regretted his earlier מצוות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ordinary sin would just go on the scale next to the old merits. But someone who regrets the good he did takes back those merits, so they disappear from the scale. That is why he loses 'the earlier ones.'

keyTerms.meaning: The earlier ones (his earlier good deeds)

steps.whatToRemember: A person should picture himself balanced, so every act is decisive. A צדיק loses his past merits only if he regrets the good he did; a רשע who does תשובה has his past wiped away.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't conclude that one late sin wipes out a lifetime of מצוות. According to ריש לקיש, the merits are lost only because the person regrets having done them.

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said:
It is talking about one who regrets the earlier ones.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ: בְּתוֹהֶא עַל הָרִאשׁוֹנוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא): limits רבי שמעון בן יוחי's ruling to a specific situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the case was a צדיק who simply sinned at the end, so his past merits should still count.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is a צדיק who regrets his earlier מצוות, so those merits are taken away and not counted.

steps.title: The three-strand cord: Bible, משנה and proper conduct
steps.stepSummary: The משנה teaches that a person involved in מקרא, משנה and דרך ארץ will not quickly sin. Someone with none of the three is not part of civilized society.
steps.simpleTranslation: Anyone who has Bible, משנה and proper conduct will not sin quickly, as the פסוק says, 'A threefold cord is not quickly broken.' Anyone who has none of these is not part of society.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It says that three good things together protect a person from sin, and lacking all three puts a person outside civilized society.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה compares the person to a rope made of three strands. Each strand (Bible, משנה, proper conduct) adds strength, so together they are hard to break. The second half is the reverse case: with no strands at all, the person is not considered a proper member of society.

keyTerms.meaning: Bible, the written תורה and the rest of תנ"ך
Proper conduct: honest work and decent behavior
A threefold cord, a rope of three strands
He is not part of civilized society

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
Anyone who is involved in Bible
and in Mishnah and in proper conduct
will not quickly sin,
as it says: “And the threefold cord
is not quickly broken.”
And anyone who is involved neither in Bible
nor in Mishnah nor in proper conduct
is not part of civilized society.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ כֹּל שֶׁיֶּשְׁנוֹ בַּמִּקְרָא וּבַמִּשְׁנָה וּבְדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה begins. It moves from the earlier discussion of merit and sin to what protects a person from sinning.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Bible, משנה and proper conduct together protect a person from sin. Lacking all three puts him outside civilized society.

steps.title: Why the righteous suffer in this world
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק compares צדיקים to a tree standing in a pure place whose branches hang over an impure place. Cutting the branches leaves the whole tree in purity. In the same way, suffering in this world clears away a צדיק's few sins so he inherits all of עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: The righteous are like a tree standing in a pure place with branches hanging over an impure place. Cut the branches, and the whole tree is in a pure place. So too, הקדוש ברוך הוא brings suffering on the righteous in this world so they will inherit עולם הבא, as it says, 'Your beginning was small, but your end will be very great.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins with a teaching of רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק. He uses a tree parable to explain why good people suffer in this world.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The tree is the צדיק. Most of it is in a pure place, which stands for his many good deeds. The branches over the impure place are his few sins. Suffering in this world 'cuts off' those sins, so his reward in עולם הבא is complete.

keyTerms.meaning: Are compared to, as in a parable
Its branches, the top of the tree

steps.confusionAlert: The tree does not stand for a mostly sinful person. It stands for someone almost entirely righteous, and only the small 'branch' part, his few sins, is dealt with through suffering.

phrases.aramaic: גְּמָ׳ אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי צָדוֹק:
phrases.english: GEMARA: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok said:
To what are the righteous compared in this world?
To a tree that stands entirely in a pure place,
and its branches lean over an impure place.
If its branches are cut off,
it stands entirely in a pure place.

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מֵבִיא יִסּוּרִים
phrases.english: So too, the Holy One, Blessed be He, brings suffering
upon the righteous in this world,
so that they will inherit the World to Come,
as it says: “And your beginning was small,
but your end will greatly increase.”

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי צָדוֹק: לְמָה צַדִּיקִים נִמְשָׁלִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא opens its discussion after the משנה with an אגדה about how צדיקים are treated in this world.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Suffering in this world cleans away a צדיק's few sins so he receives complete reward in עולם הבא.

steps.title: Why the wicked prosper in this world
steps.stepSummary: The mirror image: רשעים are like a tree standing in an impure place whose branches hang over a pure place. Good in this world pays them for their few good deeds, so they are left fully in the 'impure' place for the next world.
steps.simpleTranslation: The wicked are like a tree standing in an impure place with branches hanging over a pure place. Cut the branches, and the whole tree is in an impure place. So too, הקדוש ברוך הוא gives good to the wicked in this world in order to drive them out and send them down to the lowest level, as it says, 'There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the ways of death.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק continues with the opposite parable. It explains why wicked people sometimes do well in this world.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the tree is mostly in an impure place, which stands for the many sins. The branches over the pure place are a רשע's few good deeds. Giving him good in this world pays off those few merits now, so nothing good is left to protect him later.

keyTerms.meaning: Pours out good, gives plenty of good

steps.whatToRemember: The two parables are mirror images. צדיקים pay for their few sins here so they get all the reward later. רשעים get paid for their few good deeds here, so they get only punishment later.

phrases.english: And to what are the wicked compared in this world?
To a tree that stands entirely in an impure place
and its branches lean over a pure place.
If its branches are cut off,
it stands entirely in an impure place.

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְשַׁפֵּיעַ לָהֶן טוֹבָה
phrases.english: So too, the Holy One, Blessed be He, pours out good for them,
for the wicked, in this world
in order to drive them out and bring them down
to the lowest level,
as it says: “There is a way that seems straight to a man,
but its end is the ways of death.”

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְמָה רְשָׁעִים דּוֹמִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the mirror-image parable to complete רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק's teaching.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Good in this world pays off a רשע's few merits, leaving him with only punishment in the future.

steps.title: The elders in Lod ask: is learning or doing greater?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tells a story. רבי טרפון and the elders were gathered in an upper room in לוד, and the question was raised whether learning or doing is greater.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once רבי טרפון and the elders were reclining in the upper room of the house of Nitzah in לוד. This question was asked before them: Is learning greater, or is doing greater?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up a story and presents the question the sages discussed. The answers come in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question fits the משנה's praise of learning מקרא and משנה. The issue is which ranks higher: תלמוד (learning) or מעשה (actually doing the מצוות).

phrases.english: And once, Rabbi Tarfon and the elders were
reclining in the upper room of the house of Nitzah in Lod.
This question was asked before them:
Is learning greater, or is doing greater?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּכְבָר הָיָה רַבִּי טַרְפוֹן וּזְקֵנִים מְסוּבִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new story connected to the משנה's emphasis on Torah study.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which is greater: Torah learning or actually doing the מצוות?

steps.title: רבי טרפון says doing; רבי עקיבא says learning
steps.stepSummary: רבי טרפון answers that doing is greater, and רבי עקיבא answers that learning is greater.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי טרפון answered: Doing is greater. רבי עקיבא answered: Learning is greater.
steps.whatsHappening: Two great sages give opposite answers to the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי טרפון puts the focus on action, the actual fulfilling of the מצוות. רבי עקיבא puts the focus on learning. The disagreement sets up the group's final decision.

phrases.aramaic: נַעֲנָה רַבִּי טַרְפוֹן וְאָמַר: מַעֲשֶׂה גָּדוֹל.
phrases.english: Rabbi Tarfon answered and said: Doing is greater.

phrases.aramaic: נַעֲנָה רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא וְאָמַר: תַּלְמוּד גָּדוֹל.
phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva answered and said: Learning is greater.

steps.triggerLanguage: נַעֲנָה רַבִּי טַרְפוֹן וְאָמַר: מַעֲשֶׂה גָּדוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the two opposing answers to the question just asked.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי טרפון: doing is greater. רבי עקיבא: learning is greater.

steps.title: Everyone agrees: learning is greater because it leads to doing
steps.stepSummary: All the sages concluded that learning is greater, because learning brings a person to action.
steps.simpleTranslation: Everyone answered and said: Learning is greater, because learning leads to doing.
steps.whatsHappening: The whole group decides the question. They side with רבי עקיבא but give a reason that also honors רבי טרפון's point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Learning wins, but its greatness comes from where it leads, which is action. So the conclusion joins the two views: תלמוד ranks higher because it is the source of מעשה.
steps.whatToRemember: Learning is greater than doing, but only because learning brings a person to do the מצוות.
steps.whyThisMatters: This conclusion is a famous guide for priorities in Jewish life. Learning comes first because it is what produces proper action.

phrases.english: They all answered and said: Learning is greater,
because learning leads to doing.

steps.triggerLanguage: נַעֲנוּ כּוּלָּם וְאָמְרוּ: תַּלְמוּד גָּדוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles the disagreement between רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Learning is greater, because learning leads to action.

steps.title: רבי יוסי: Torah learning came years before the land-based מצוות
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא from רבי יוסי supports the idea that learning is great by showing it came 40 years before חלה, 54 years before תרומות and מעשרות, 61 years before שמיטה, and 103 years before יובל.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: רבי יוסי says learning is great, because it came before חלה by forty years, before תרומות and מעשרות by fifty-four years, before שמיטה years by sixty-one years, and before יובל years by one hundred and three years.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that backs up the conclusion that learning is great. רבי יוסי shows that the Torah was learned long before many מצוות could even be kept.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah was given in the מדבר, but many מצוות only started once the Jews were in ארץ ישראל. רבי יוסי counts the years between them. Learning came first in time, and he uses that to show how great it is.

keyTerms.meaning: The portion of dough given to a כהן
Gifts and tithes taken from produce
The seventh year, when the land rests
The fiftieth year, when slaves go free and fields return to their owners

phrases.english: It is taught in a ברייתא: Rabbi Yosei says:
Learning is great,
for it came before חלה by forty years,
phrases.notes: The Torah was given soon after leaving מצרים, but חלה only started once they entered the land, forty years later.

phrases.english: before תרומות and מעשרות by fifty-four years,
phrases.notes: These started only after another fourteen years of conquering and dividing the land: 40 + 14 = 54.

phrases.english: before the שמיטה years by sixty-one years,
and before the יובל years by one hundred and three years.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: גָּדוֹל תַּלְמוּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the conclusion of step 11 that learning is greater.
steps.raayaObject: That Torah learning is great and comes first
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא of רבי יוסי counting the years between מתן תורה and the land-based מצוות

steps.title: The math for יובל seems off by one year
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the number 103: if תרומות began after 54 years and יובל comes 50 years later, the total should be 104.
steps.simpleTranslation: One hundred and three? It should be one hundred and four!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא checks רבי יוסי's numbers and finds what looks like a mistake. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The count of years for יובל began when the land was divided, 54 years after מתן תורה. Adding 50 years gives 104, not 103. So why did רבי יוסי say 103?

keyTerms.meaning: They are / it comes out to

phrases.english: One hundred and three?
It comes out to one hundred and four!
phrases.notes: 54 years until the land was divided, plus 50 years for the יובל cycle, equals 104.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵאָה וְשָׁלֹשׁ? מֵאָה וְאַרְבַּע הָוְיָין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the last number in רבי יוסי's ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Simple addition (54 + 50) gives 104, so 103 seems wrong.

steps.title: יובל takes effect at the start of its year
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי יוסי holds the יובל releases from the very beginning of the fiftieth year, so only 49 full years pass after the 54.
steps.simpleTranslation: He holds that the יובל releases from its very beginning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the number 103. רבי יוסי holds that the יובל year starts working right away, the moment it begins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the יובל only counted after the whole fiftieth year, we would get 104. But since its release takes effect as soon as the fiftieth year starts, only 49 full years have passed: 54 + 49 = 103.

keyTerms.meaning: He holds / is of the opinion

phrases.english: He holds: the יובל releases from its very beginning.
phrases.notes: So the release happens right when the fiftieth year begins, after 49 full years. That's 54 + 49 = 103.

steps.triggerLanguage: קָסָבַר: יוֹבֵל מִתְּחִילָּתוֹ הוּא מְשַׁמֵּט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the math challenge of step 13.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The יובל only counts after the full fiftieth year, giving 104.
steps.terutzMaskana: The יובל releases from its start, so 103 is correct.

steps.title: A person is judged first on Torah learning
steps.stepSummary: Just as learning comes before action, judgment for learning comes before judgment for action, as רב המנונא taught from the פסוק in משלי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Just as learning comes before action, so too judgment for it comes before judgment for action, like רב המנונא. For רב המנונא said: A person's judgment begins only with words of Torah, as it says: 'One who lets out water is the beginning of strife.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second way learning comes first: in the heavenly judgment, a person is asked about Torah learning before anything else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 12 showed learning came first in time. Now we learn it also comes first in judgment. רב המנונא reads the פסוק as saying the first 'case' against a person is about Torah, which is compared to water.

keyTerms.meaning: Strife / a case brought against someone

phrases.english: And just as learning comes before action,
so too its judgment comes before the judgment for action,
like the teaching of Rav Hamnuna.
For Rav Hamnuna said:
The beginning of a person's judgment is not
about anything but words of Torah,
as it says: "One who lets out water is the beginning of strife."
phrases.notes: משלי 17:14. Water here stands for Torah, so letting it go (not learning) is the first charge.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּכְשֵׁם שֶׁהַלִּימּוּד קוֹדֵם לְמַעֲשֶׂה כָּךְ דִּינוֹ קוֹדֵם לְמַעֲשֶׂה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends 'learning comes first' from time to judgment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In Heaven, a person is judged first about Torah learning.

steps.title: The reward for Torah learning also comes first
steps.stepSummary: Just as judgment for learning comes first, so does the reward for learning, as shown from the פסוק in תהלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And just as its judgment comes before action, so too its reward comes before action, as it says: 'And He gave them the lands of nations, and they inherited the labor of peoples, so that they would keep His statutes and guard His teachings.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes with a third way learning comes first: its reward is given before the reward for doing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pattern builds: first in time, first in judgment, and now first in reward. The פסוק lists 'keeping His statutes' first, which the גמרא understands as referring to Torah learning, so its reward is mentioned first.
steps.whatToRemember: Learning comes first in three ways: it came first in history, a person is judged on it first, and its reward comes first.

phrases.english: And just as its judgment comes before action,
so too its reward comes before the reward for action,
as it says: "And He gave them the lands of nations,
and they inherited the labor of peoples,
so that they would keep His statutes
phrases.notes: תהלים 105:44–45. 'Keeping' comes first in the פסוק, and the גמרא reads it as learning.

phrases.english: and guard His teachings."

steps.triggerLanguage: וּכְשֵׁם שֶׁדִּינוֹ קוֹדֵם לְמַעֲשֶׂה כָּךְ שְׂכָרוֹ קוֹדֵם לְמַעֲשֶׂה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the pattern from judgment to reward.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The reward for Torah learning comes before the reward for doing מצוות.

steps.title: A person with no Torah and no proper conduct cannot be a witness
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's line about someone with no מקרא and no משנה. רבי יוחנן adds that such a person is also פסול לעדות.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'Anyone who has neither Bible nor משנה' (nor proper conduct is not part of society). רבי יוחנן said: And he is also disqualified from being a witness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the last line of the משנה and quotes it. רבי יוחנן adds a practical legal result: such a person may not testify.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only said this person is 'not part of society,' which sounds like a moral statement. רבי יוחנן turns it into a legal ruling: he is disqualified from giving testimony. Someone with no Torah and no proper conduct is not trusted to tell the truth in court.

keyTerms.meaning: The study of the Oral Torah teachings

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that lacking Torah and proper conduct has real legal results, and is not only a matter of reputation.

phrases.english: Anyone who has no Bible
phrases.notes: This quotes the end of our משנה, which goes on: 'and no proper conduct, is not part of society.'

phrases.english: and no משנה,
Rabbi Yochanan said:
And he is disqualified from testimony.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֹּל שֶׁאֵינוֹ לֹא בַּמִּקְרָא וְלֹא בַּמִּשְׁנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion about the greatness of learning and goes back to the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person with no מקרא, no משנה and no proper conduct is disqualified from being a witness.

steps.title: Eating in the marketplace is like a dog, and some say it disqualifies a witness
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that someone who eats in the marketplace is compared to a dog. A second opinion adds that he is disqualified from testimony.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: One who eats in the marketplace is like a dog. And some say he is disqualified from being a witness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with another example of improper conduct, eating in the marketplace, and two opinions about how serious it is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion only shames this behavior by comparing the person to a dog. The 'some say' opinion goes further and gives a legal result: like the person in רבי יוחנן's ruling, he cannot be a witness. Someone who is not embarrassed to act this way in public is not trusted to be careful with the truth.
steps.confusionAlert: There are two opinions here. 'Like a dog' is the first view, a strong criticism. 'Disqualified from testimony' is a separate, stricter view.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who eats in the marketplace
is comparable to a dog.
And some say
he is disqualified from testimony.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הָאוֹכֵל בַּשּׁוּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of improper conduct making a person unfit to testify, with a new example.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eating in the marketplace is like the behavior of a dog. According to the יש אומרים it also disqualifies a person from testimony.

steps.title: The הלכה follows the stricter opinion
steps.stepSummary: רבי אידי בר אבין rules that the הלכה follows the יש אומרים: one who eats in the marketplace is disqualified from testimony.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rabbi Idi bar Avin said: The הלכה follows the 'some say' opinion.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא decides between the two opinions in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא left two views open. רבי אידי בר אבין decides the practical law: eating in the marketplace is more than shameful. It actually makes a person unfit to be a witness.
steps.whatToRemember: Two kinds of people are unfit to testify because of their behavior: someone with no Torah and no proper conduct (רבי יוחנן), and someone who eats in the marketplace (the הלכה follows יש אומרים).

phrases.english: Rabbi Idi bar Avin said:
The halacha is in accordance with 'some say.'

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲלָכָה כְּיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the argument presented in the ברייתא.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: One who eats in the marketplace is disqualified from testimony.

steps.title: בר קפרא begins a teaching about an angry person
steps.stepSummary: בר קפרא opens a new teaching about a רגזן, an angry person. The teaching continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: בר קפרא taught: An angry person (the rest of his teaching continues next).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It introduces a new teaching from בר קפרא about an angry person, which is completed in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only the opening word, 'an angry person,' appears here. It continues the list of bad character traits and their results, but what בר קפרא says about this person comes in the continuation.

phrases.english: Bar Kappara taught:
An angry person

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּרַשׁ בַּר קַפָּרָא: רַגְזָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from bad behavior that affects testimony to a new teaching about the trait of anger.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The teaching about the angry person begins here and is completed on the next amud.
